div.h1: Odoo implementation with a predictable path
div.p: Structured architecture, community good practice, and a delivery plan with durations, named deliverables and stated responsibilities on both sides.
Each phase closes with something you can hold, and you can stop between phases. That is the only guarantee that genuinely protects a buyer.

div.h2: What we need from your team
div.p: The single largest difference between a project that lands on time and one that does not.

ul.li: A decision maker who can settle a process disagreement in the same week
One key user per area with real hours reserved, not hours in addition to a full job
Access to your current data, however messy it is
Someone who owns the product and tax records, because that is where projects stall
Willingness to change a process when the standard is better than your habit
A named team, with the same people through the project
Code review on every merge and automated tests on what we build
Your repository, accessible to you from the first week
A weekly report short enough that you will actually read it
Presence through your first fiscal and accounting close

div.p: A focused project on one operation with a simple fiscal profile is a matter of weeks per phase. A multi-company industrial operation issuing documents in several states is a matter of months. Anyone who quotes a duration before discovery is guessing, and the guess is always padded.

What drives the number, what the contract models are and a benchmark you can check us against are on the investment page . We would rather send you there than write a number here that turns out to be wrong for your case.

t.t-value: 'You do not have to buy an implementation to find out whether Odoo fits. Discovery is a deliverable in its own right, and it is yours to use with anyone.'

div.h1: Development that survives the next upgrade
div.p: Code review on every merge, automated tests, continuous integration, and a policy of pushing generic work upstream so the community maintains it instead of you.

div.h2: First we check whether it already exists
div.p: Reviewing hundreds of community contributions a year means we usually know whether a requirement is already solved. When it is, we install and configure the module rather than quoting development for it.
This costs us billable hours on purpose. A client who discovers a year later that they paid to rebuild something that shipped for free does not stay a client.
The same process we use on the community repositories, applied to your private code.
No engineer merges their own work. Every change is read by someone else before it can reach your system.
Business logic ships with tests. It is what lets us upgrade your custom modules later without discovering the breakage in production.
Every commit runs the linters and the test suite. A red build does not get deployed, regardless of the deadline.
Source in a repository you have access to, with readable history. Not a zip file at the end of the project.
We inherit and extend rather than editing the core. That is the difference between a system you can upgrade and one you cannot.
If what we built for you is generic, we offer to contribute it. You keep your competitive logic private and stop paying to maintain the plumbing.

div.p: We also review other people's code as a service. If you inherited a customised Odoo and want to know what is in it, that is a second opinion or a standardisation job.

Hour packages, bought in blocks and consumed against a backlog you prioritise. Each item is estimated before it starts, and you approve the estimate. Consumption is reported monthly with what was delivered against it.

Small, well defined items can be quoted individually at a fixed price. Large initiatives are broken into phases, which is slower to sell and much better for both sides. The contract models in detail .

div.p: Managed hosting with monitoring, stated backup retention and a recovery objective in writing. In a region you choose.

div.h2: The specifics, since they are the point

div.p: Containerised deployment on a major cloud provider, in a Brazilian region by default. Another region, or your own data centre, on request — the deployment recipe is portable by design.
Daily automated database and file store backups, retained off-site, with a restore tested periodically rather than assumed to work.
Availability, response time, disk, queue depth and failed jobs, watched around the clock with alerting to an on-call engineer.
Production plus a staging copy on request, so a change can be validated on your real data before it reaches the people using it.
Encryption in transit, restricted network access, named accounts with no shared credentials, and patching as part of the service rather than as a project.
Agreed in the contract with the measurement window and the exclusions written down. A number without a measurement method is marketing.

div.h2: Why take hosting from the same team
div.p: When the application team and the infrastructure team are different companies, every slow page becomes a debate about whose fault it is. Here it is one number to call, and the person who answers can read the code and the server metrics in the same session.
And because the deployment recipe lives in your repository, taking hosting from us does not lock you in. Another team can stand up an identical environment elsewhere. How that works .

t.t-value: 'Tell us the current setup, the database size and the user count. We come back with a sizing, a price and a migration window.'

div.p: Process before technology. An ERP installed on top of a process nobody agrees on just makes the disagreement faster and more expensive.
The process as it actually runs, including the spreadsheet somebody maintains at home and the approval that happens by message. Not the process in the manual.
Rework, waiting, double entry, decisions taken without data. Named, located and where possible quantified.
The process as it should run, designed against what the platform does well rather than against what your current system forced you into.
Who executes, who approves, who is consulted and who is informed, for every step. Most process failures are accountability failures wearing a technical costume.
What to measure, where the number comes from, who looks at it and what they are expected to do when it moves.
How the process is kept alive after the consultants leave, which is the part almost every engagement skips.

ul.li: Current and future state process diagrams, in a format your team can edit
A responsibility matrix per process step
An indicator sheet with sources and owners
A prioritised list of changes, separated into process changes and system changes
A short executive summary that can go to a board without translation

div.p: A single process area is a matter of weeks. A full operation is longer, and we would rather scope it by area so you see value before the end.

The deliverable stands alone. If you then want the system built on top of it, it becomes the discovery phase of an implementation and you do not pay for that phase twice. If you take it to another supplier, it still works — it is your document.

div.h1: A second opinion on your Odoo
div.p: We review another supplier's proposal, or audit an Odoo somebody else implemented. Fixed scope, fixed price, and no obligation to change anything.

You have a proposal in front of you and no way to judge it. We read it and tell you what is missing, what is over-specified, which requirements are already solved by existing modules, and which line items you should ask about.
We do not tell you to hire us instead. That would make this worthless.

Your system works, mostly, and you have no idea whether it is well built. We audit the installation and tell you what state it is in, what risk it carries at the next upgrade, and what would improve it most per unit of money.
If your current supplier is doing a good job, we will say so in writing.

div.h2: Check your current partnership yourself, for free
div.p: Six questions. If you cannot answer three of them, that is worth a conversation.

ol.li: Can you open the repository with your custom code right now, without asking anyone?
Does anyone review the code before it reaches your production system?
Do you know which of your modules are standard, which are community and which are proprietary custom?
Do you know what your next version upgrade will cost, and why?
Could another supplier take over your system without rebuilding it?
When you ask for something, do you get an estimate before the work starts?

div.p: Tell us whether you have a proposal to review or a system to audit, and we come back with the scope and the price.

t.t-value: 'What do you want reviewed, and what is worrying you?'

div.p: Training for the people who will build, configure and operate Odoo. Taught by the engineers who maintain the modules, which is a different thing from reading the documentation aloud.
The Odoo framework, module structure, extension without modification, tests, and how to contribute to a community repository. The last part is what makes a developer employable beyond one company.
Process design in Odoo, configuration depth per application, the Brazilian fiscal model, and how to tell the difference between a requirement and a habit.
Your own people, on your own data, in your own configuration. Generic training on a demo database is the reason people go back to spreadsheets.

ul.li: Self-paced courses in our online catalogue
Live remote sessions with exercises and a real environment
In-company training, on your configuration
Mentoring for an internal team taking over an Odoo

div.h2: Why we run this at all
div.p: Brazil has far more Odoo projects than Odoo engineers, and the shortage is the main reason projects fail. Training people who may end up working for our clients, our competitors or on their own is still better for us than a market where Odoo has a reputation for failing.
It is the same logic as contributing upstream, applied to people instead of code.
